doc.title: Eddie Metz Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, October 3, 2015

title: Dixieland, Wild Bill Davison and Bobby Hackett
summary: Eddie Condon's quip, why Dixieland is dismissed, playing with Wild Bill Davison and his father's recording with Hackett.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Right. And I think the younger guys have a problem with it because it’s so diatonic. When you’re playing Dixieland there’s not too many sharp nines or flat nines or flat fives. You know Eddie Condon used to say, “those modern guys, they flat their fifths. We drink our fifths.” You know that was a famous Eddie Condon quote. But I think that part of history, the improvised six or seven piece band, like at the jazz parties, watching that video last night. That was great. I loved seeing that. And I’d love to get a copy of that sometime. It’s being forgotten about.
To me, I’ve got this idea that most of it is too happy to be taken seriously as an art form.
Yeah. It is a happy music.
And for some reason the scholars and so forth, it doesn’t have enough I don’t know, trauma to it or something.

Well and some players think it’s too constraining harmonically. But I played with Wild Bill Davison several times. Oh my God, it was unbelievable. His energy and the way he would lead the band through an out chorus, it was outrageous. Pee Wee Erwin was the same way. Warren Vache can do it. And that’s the bag he was coming out of. Warren grew up listening to Bobby Hackett. Nobody remembers who Bobby Hackett was anymore. Oh my gosh.
Well someone does. Rossano yesterday says —

Yeah right. And luckily I’ve been able to play with people who — my dad got to play with Hackett one time and they actually did a little recording. It came out years later. It’s like he would start every song by clicking his ring on the bell for the tempo. So the band could hear it over the crowd talking. This little kind of clinking sound. Everybody knew where the tempo was. And Ernie Hackett was playing drums on there. I did go one night to see that. That was at the Ponchartrain in Detroit.
